mentions.quote: for Rakshasas plunder a *śrāddha* that is devoid of protection
mentions.role: antagonist — demonic beings who spoil unprotected ancestral rites

mentions.quote: What one eats with his head covered, what he eats facing south, and what he eats with his shoes on—that the Rakshasas indeed eat
mentions.role: antagonist — consume improperly eaten food

mentions.quote: A tear sends the offering to the departed spirits, anger to one's enemies, falsehood to dogs, a touch of the foot to the Rakshasas
mentions.role: recipient of ritually contaminated offerings

mentions.quote: One should not perform a *śrāddha* at night, for the night is declared to be of the nature of Rakshasas
mentions.role: symbolic — nighttime identified with Rakshasa nature

entities.description: Demonic beings (Rakshasas) who plunder śrāddha rites lacking divine protection and consume food eaten with ritual impropriety.
entities.justification: Rakshasas appear four times in p-8b8ea4 as the primary demonic threat to the ancestral rite, framing the protective structure of the Vaiśvadeva ritual sequence.

mentions.quote: Having first performed the rite of propitiation to Agni, Soma, and Yama, he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors
mentions.role: primary deity propitiated at the opening of the śrāddha fire rite

mentions.quote: But in the absence of a fire, he should place the offering in the hand of a Brahmana; for that Brahmana who is a seer of sacred formulas is declared by the wise to be the fire
mentions.role: symbolic referent — Brahmana equated with Agni when fire is absent

mentions.quote: He should always offer the Agnihotra at the beginning and end of the day and night
mentions.role: recipient of the daily Agnihotra fire oblation

entities.description: The Vedic fire deity Agni, propitiated first in the śrāddha sequence and associated with the sacred fires that householders must maintain daily.
entities.justification: Agni is named as the first deity propitiated in p-8b8ea4 and the Agnihotra to Agni recurs as the cornerstone of daily household sacrifice throughout this window.

mentions.quote: Having first performed the rite of propitiation to Agni, Soma, and Yama
mentions.role: deity propitiated alongside Agni at the opening of the śrāddha

mentions.quote: The food of sages, milk, Soma, meat which has not been prepared with spices … is called a natural oblation
mentions.role: sacred substance classified as a natural oblation

entities.description: Soma is both a Vedic deity propitiated in the śrāddha rite and a sacred substance classified among natural oblations appropriate for ancestral offerings.
entities.justification: Soma appears in p-8b8ea4 first as a deity in the triadic propitiation formula (Agni–Soma–Yama) and then as a natural food-oblation, showing its dual divine-material status.

mentions.quote: Having first performed the rite of propitiation to Agni, Soma, and Yama, he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors
mentions.role: deity of death propitiated to protect and validate the ancestral rite

entities.description: Yama, the Vedic god of death and the dead, is propitiated in the opening phase of the śrāddha fire rite as the deity who governs the realm of the ancestors.
entities.justification: Yama is named in p-8b8ea4 as the third member of the opening propitiatory triad, reflecting his role as lord of the ancestors who are the rite's intended beneficiaries.

mentions.quote: Whatever food is presented that has been released from both hands, that the evil-minded Asuras forcibly plunder
mentions.role: antagonist — demonic beings who seize food improperly offered with both hands released

entities.description: Asuras are demonic adversaries who forcibly plunder food that is presented incorrectly (released from both hands) during the śrāddha, constituting a ritual danger parallel to that of the Rakshasas.
entities.justification: The Asuras appear in p-8b8ea4 as the specific demonic threat associated with improper hand-posture during food offering, providing a demonic rationale for the ritual technicality.

mentions.quote: Or the grandfather may eat at that *śrāddha*, as Manu has declared
mentions.role: law-giver invoked as authority for a specific śrāddha rule

mentions.quote: Manu has declared an occasional `anadhyāya` in these cases
mentions.role: law-giver cited as authority for the rule on anadhyāya during meteorological events

entities.description: Manu is the primordial law-giver and author of this text, cited internally as an authority for specific injunctions on śrāddha procedure and forbidden days for Vedic study.
entities.justification: The text refers to 'Manu has declared' in two places within p-8b8ea4, treating its own author as an in-text authority, which is a distinctive feature of the Manusmṛti's self-referential jurisprudence.

mentions.quote: They call the fathers Vasus, the grandfathers Rudras, and the great-grandfathers Adityas; this is the eternal Vedic revelation
mentions.role: divine classes with whom the three generations of paternal ancestors are identified

entities.description: The Vasus, Rudras, and Adityas are groups of Vedic deities with whom the three paternal generations (fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers) are respectively identified in ancestral rites.
entities.justification: In p-8b8ea4 (Mn_3.284) the text explicitly equates the three paternal generations with the three major divine groups — Vasus, Rudras, and Adityas — framing the śrāddha as an act of worship of deified ancestors.

mentions.quote: A Chandala, a pig, a rooster, and also a dog, a menstruating woman, and a eunuch must not see the twice-born as they eat
mentions.role: polluting presence forbidden from viewing the sacred meal

mentions.quote: He should not live with outcastes, nor with Chandalas, nor with Pulkasas
mentions.role: group whose proximity is prohibited for the Brahmana householder

entities.description: Chandalas are an outcaste group ritually classified as polluting — their gaze during the śrāddha meal invalidates the offering, and cohabitation with them is forbidden.
entities.justification: Chandalas appear twice in p-8b8ea4 in two separate functional contexts: ritual pollution of the śrāddha (Mn_3.239) and the rules on forbidden residence (Mn_4.79), marking them as a key structuring category of ritual and social purity.

mentions.quote: One should honor them with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with the rite for the gods
mentions.role: honored guests who officiate and receive at the śrāddha

mentions.quote: for that Brahmana who is a seer of sacred formulas is declared by the wise to be the fire
mentions.role: substitute for the sacred fire in the absence of an actual fire

mentions.quote: A Brahmana *snātaka* who is able should never perish from hunger
mentions.role: subject of rules for the Brahmana householder's livelihood and conduct

entities.description: Brahmanas are the priestly varna whose presence, knowledge, and ritual purity constitute the central requirement for valid śrāddha and sacrificial rites throughout this window.
entities.justification: Brahmanas are the most pervasive group in this window (spanning indices 137–179), appearing as ritual officiant, recipient, sacred-fire surrogate, and the subject of extensive conduct rules, making them the dominant social-ritual category of the text.

mentions.quote: He who, after eating at a *śrāddha*, gives the leftovers to a Shudra, that fool goes headlong to the hell called Kalasutra
mentions.role: prohibited recipient of śrāddha leftovers

mentions.quote: He should not give advice to a Shudra, nor give him leftovers, nor what has been offered as an oblation; he should not teach him Dharma
mentions.role: person to whom the Brahmana must not extend religious teaching or ritual food

mentions.quote: one should not go with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with Shudras
mentions.role: group forbidden as travel companions for the Brahmana snātaka

entities.description: Shudras are the fourth varna whose contact with sacred ritual substances (śrāddha leftovers, oblations) is prohibited, and to whom the transmission of Dharma is forbidden.
entities.justification: Shudras appear across multiple paragraphs (p-8b8ea4, p-4c50dc) as a recurring negative boundary — their contact with ritual food, sacred knowledge, and Brahmana travel company is systematically prohibited.

mentions.quote: For their protection, one should first perform the rite for the gods; for Rakshasas plunder a *śrāddha* that is devoid of protection
Then, with a concentrated mind, having made three *piṇḍas* from the remainder of the oblation, one should offer them facing south

themes.justification: The dominant theme of the window's opening section (p-8b8ea4, Mn_3.204–286) is the step-by-step procedure of the ancestral śrāddha rite — its spatial, ritual, and protective requirements — framed by the need to guard offerings from demonic disruption.

mentions.quote: A Chandala, a pig, a rooster, and also a dog, a menstruating woman, and a eunuch must not see the twice-born as they eat
A pig destroys it by its smell, a rooster by the wind from its wings, a dog by its glance, and a man of a lower caste by his touch

themes.justification: A sustained preoccupation in this window is the various vectors of ritual contamination — animal presence, bodily states, caste proximity — that can void the sacred meal; this logic of ritual pollution structures dozens of injunctions.

themes.topic: Anadhyāya: forbidden periods for Vedic study

mentions.quote: There is an *anadhyāya* when a crowd of people is weeping
During a fog, when the sound of arrows is heard, at both twilights, on the new moon day, the fourteenth day, the full moon day, and on the *aṣṭakā* days
When the sound of the Samaveda is heard, one should never study the Rigveda or the Yajurveda

themes.justification: Paragraphs 138–157 (p-e69207 through p-608247) constitute a dense catalogue of anadhyāya — natural, celestial, and social occasions that suspend Vedic recitation — making this a major topical cluster within the window.

mentions.quote: He should move about in this world, conforming his dress, speech, and intellect to his age, occupation, wealth, sacred learning, and family
One should not despise oneself on account of past failures; until death one should seek good fortune and not think it difficult to obtain
One should speak the truth, one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak an unpleasant truth

themes.justification: A large portion of this window (roughly Mn_4.1–4.149) is devoted to the daily behavioral code for the Brahmana householder-snātaka — governing livelihood, bodily conduct, speech, travel, and ethical deportment.

themes.topic: Hell (naraka) as consequence of ritual transgression

mentions.quote: He who, after eating at a *śrāddha*, gives the leftovers to a Shudra, that fool goes headlong to the hell called Kalasutra
`Tāmisra`, `Andhatāmisra`, `Mahāraurava`, and `Raurava`, the hell called `Kālasūtra`, and `Mahānaraka` as well
He who explains Dharma to him, and he who enjoins a vow upon him, sinks with him into that hell named `Asaṃvṛta`

themes.justification: Multiple named hells — Kalasutra, Tāmisra, Asaṃvṛta, and seventeen others — are invoked throughout this window as deterrents for specific transgressions, constituting an eschatological sanction structure underlying the ritual code.

themes.topic: Veda study as Brahmana's highest duty

mentions.quote: He should always study the Veda at the proper time, without weariness; for they call that his highest Dharma; what is other is called a secondary Dharma
Through constant study of the Veda, through purity, and through *tapas*, and through non-enmity towards beings, one remembers one's former birth
Remembering one's former birth, one studies the Veda again; and by the constant study of the Veda, one enjoys endless happiness

themes.justification: The window closes (indices 175–179, p-6ac1c1 through p-6913bc) with a culminating statement that Vedic study is the Brahmana's highest Dharma and the means of recalling past births, framing all other conduct rules as subordinate to this soteriological end.

themes.topic: Livelihoods permitted and forbidden for Brahmanas

mentions.quote: `Ṛta` is to be known as gleaning; `amṛta` is what is received unsolicited; `mṛta` is begging for alms; and `pramṛta` is remembered as agriculture
`Satyānṛta` is trade, and by that also one may live; but service is called `śvavṛtti` (a dog's life), therefore one should avoid it
He should not accept a gift from a king who is not of royal descent, nor from those who live by a slaughterhouse, a wheel, or a banner

themes.justification: Mn_4.4–4.9 introduces a systematic typology of Brahmana livelihoods graded by ritual purity, extending through prohibitions on accepting gifts from ritually tainted sources — a sustained economic-ethical theme running through the middle of the window.

themes.topic: Karmic and ritual efficacy of gift-giving

mentions.quote: Whatever a man, filled with faith, gives according to the rule, that very thing becomes for the ancestors in the next world endless and imperishable
A gift to a seller of Soma becomes excrement; to a physician, pus and blood; what is given to a temple priest is lost; and to a usurer, it finds no firm footing

themes.justification: The text implies that the karmic value of a gift is entirely determined by the recipient's ritual status — this underlying theory of donative efficacy, though not stated as a principle, governs the entire taxonomy of worthy and unworthy Brahmana recipients.
